analysis.one_liner: Shields retirement plan managers from lawsuits for putting workers' 401(k) money into crypto, hedge funds, and private equity.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have made it easier to put 401(k) money into crypto, hedge funds, and private equity with less legal risk for plan managers, never received a committee vote and died at the end of the Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal retirement law (ERISA), the people who manage 401(k) plans can be sued for breach of duty if they pick bad investments. This bill would have said plan managers cannot be sued solely for offering employees a menu of speculative assets — cryptocurrency, hedge funds, private equity, venture capital, commodities, real estate, and annuities [S2][S3]. That would open the door for the financial industry to sell these high-fee, high-risk products to retirement savers. The bill never got so much as a committee vote; it was referred to the Senate HELP Committee on the day it was introduced and died there when the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be financial firms that sell alternative investments: crypto companies, private equity and hedge fund managers, and insurance companies that sell annuities. Retirement plans hold trillions of dollars, and the bill would remove the main legal deterrent — fiduciary liability — that has kept most plan managers from offering these products. Plan managers themselves would also gain protection from lawsuits. Workers would gain nothing they cannot already get: employees who want to speculate can usually do so through brokerage windows in their own plans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Crypto, private equity, and hedge fund firms

how_it_helps.text: It specifies that a plan fiduciary cannot be sued for breach of duty solely for recommending, selecting, or monitoring a wide list of asset classes — including crypto, hedge funds, private equity, venture capital, commodities, and annuities — as plan options.
It covers not just direct investments but any fund or pooled vehicle that invests in those assets, extending legal protection to the industry's packaged products.
It states this does not create an exemption from ERISA's existing core fiduciary duties of loyalty and prudence, so other avenues of liability remain.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on the roughly 90 million workers with 401(k)-style retirement plans. Fees on private equity, hedge fund, and annuity products are far higher than on ordinary index funds and are deducted from savers' returns, and volatile assets like cryptocurrency could produce large losses that the bill's sponsors frame as acceptable investment risk borne by the saver.

drawbacks.text: The bill's core effect is to reduce fiduciary liability for putting retirement money into volatile or opaque investments — digital assets like cryptocurrency, hedge funds, and private equity — which shifts the risk of losses onto workers rather than the plan managers.
Private equity, hedge funds, and annuities carry fees that are much higher than the low-cost index funds most 401(k) plans use, and those fees come directly out of savers' returns.

The liability shield applies to any 'direct or indirect' investment in a broad list of asset classes, including pooled vehicles that invest in them, which is a much wider scope than a simple clarification of existing law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost side is the serious one. Giving fiduciaries legal cover to put retirement savings into crypto, hedge funds, private equity, and annuities shifts the risk of those volatile, high-fee, hard-to-value investments onto workers, while the financial industry collects the fees. The bill does note that it creates no blanket exemption from ERISA's core duties of loyalty and prudence [S3], so a fiduciary could still be liable for other reasons — but the bill's entire purpose is to remove the main legal deterrent, liability, that keeps risky asset classes out of retirement plans. The supposed benefit — broader investment choice — is available in brokerage windows for those who want it, without the plan-level protections being loosened. On balance, the drawbacks outweigh the benefits for the people whose money is at stake.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate committee that handles retirement law, and no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended, so the bill simply expired.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 28, 2022, the final months of the 117th Congress, and immediately referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
The committee never held a markup or vote on the bill, and the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill attracted only two cosponsors, both Republicans, and no Democratic support during its three months of existence.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers' retirement savings are no worse off — the liability shield never took effect. The crypto, private equity, and hedge fund industries did not gain the access to 401(k) money the bill would have opened up.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers' retirement savings stayed under existing protections

for.name: Sen. Patrick Toomey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to shield retirement plan fiduciaries from liability for offering crypto, hedge funds, and private equity as plan options.

against.name: Department of Labor (Biden administration)
against.what_they_did: Had issued public guidance in early 2022 cautioning plan fiduciaries against putting 401(k) money into cryptocurrencies, warning of the risks to savers, setting the regulatory backdrop against which the bill was introduced.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans, and the bill's only cosponsors were the two additional Senate Republicans who signed on; no Democrat supported it.

industries.note: The bill explicitly shields fiduciaries from liability for offering digital assets in retirement plans, opening the door to flows of 401(k) money into crypto. Workers' savings would absorb the volatility and losses.

Retirement plans hold trillions of dollars, and the bill removes the liability deterrent that has kept most of it out of high-fee, lightly regulated private funds. Fees would come out of workers' returns.

industries.industry: Asset managers and insurance companies selling annuities
industries.note: The covered-investment list includes annuities and insured products plus any pooled vehicle holding the listed assets, protecting the packaged products these firms sell into 401(k) plans.
